title: The Cottingley Fairies Hoax
hook: Who really captured those tiny winged figures in 1917?
headline: The photographs that fooled a scientist

beats.label: THE CASE
beats.line: In April 1917, cousins Elsie and Frances claimed to photograph fairies in their garden.

beats.label: CLUE 1
beats.line: Doyle wrote to the editor of the spiritualist publication Light and corresponded with the cousins, not to a newspaper, calling the images genuine.

beats.label: CLUE 2
beats.line: The cousins admitted the photographs were faked with paper cutouts in the early 1980s, not in 1920.

beats.label: THE TWIST
beats.line: Later scientific analysis showed the cutouts were cardboard painted with water-colour.

end.line: Do you think the fairies were ever real?

description: Explore the famous Cottingley Fairies photos that baffled a famous author and later turned out to be a hoax.

facts.claim: In April 1917, cousins Elsie Wright and Frances Griffiths photographed alleged fairies in Cottingley.
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle publicly endorsed the photographs as genuine.
In 1920 the cousins admitted the pictures were created using paper cutouts.
Scientific analysis later identified the cutouts as cardboard painted with watercolour.
The photographs influenced public opinion and were featured in a 1920 book by Doyle.

bad: contradicted: Doyle wrote to the editor of Light and corresponded with the cousins, calling images genuine (spravne: Doyle learned of the photographs from the editor of Light but did not write to the editor; he corresponded directly with the cousins)

contradicted: The cousins admitted the photographs were faked with paper cutouts in the early 1980s (spravne: The cousins admitted the photographs were faked with cardboard cutouts in the early 1980s)
unsupported: In April 1917 cousins Elsie and Frances claimed to photograph fairies in their garden
